## Why This Is Asked

This question tests understanding of parity computation and branchless reduction techniques—skills essential in cryptography (e.g., Hamming code validation, checksums) and error-detection routines where constant-time operations matter.

## Key Concepts

- **Parity**: The XOR of all bits; 1 if an odd number of 1s, 0 if even.
- **XOR folding**: Successive shift+XOR operations collapse bit ranges without branches or loops.
- **128-bit handling**: Splitting into hi/lo halves and recombining.

## Follow-up Questions

- How would you adapt `parity128` to a 256-bit type?
- What is the time and space complexity of this approach?
- How would you make this constant-time for security-sensitive applications?

## Why This Is Asked
Constant-time 128-bit comparison is core in cryptography and DB internals to avoid timing channels; probe understanding of lexicographic, boundary handling without branches.

## Key Concepts
- Branchless logic with masks
- Lexicographic 128-bit comparison
- Handling hi/lo boundaries in constant time

## Code Example
```javascript
typedef struct { uint64_t hi; uint64_t lo; } uint128;
static inline int8_t cmp128(uint128 a, uint128 b) {
  int hi = (a.hi > b.hi) - (a.hi < b.hi); // -1,0,1
  int lo = (a.lo > b.lo) - (a.lo < b.lo);
  int m = -(int)(hi != 0); // -1 when hi != 0, else 0
  return (int8_t)((hi & m) | (lo & ~m));
}
```

## Follow-up Questions
- How would you adapt this to return a sign-agnostic 0/1/2 encoding for a hash comparison?
- Could you prove this runs in constant time regardless of inputs and compiler optimizations?
